summary:
Texas restricts trans people's use of sex-separated facilities under the Women's Privacy Act (SB 8), signed by Governor Greg Abbott on 22 September 2025 and effective 4 December 2025. Restrooms must match the sex recorded on a person's birth certificate, and the law applies to public schools, universities, prisons and Texas government buildings. Facilities face a $25,000 fine for a first violation and $125,000 for subsequent violations. The companion gender-placements statute reaches prisons only as to restroom use; it does not govern cell assignment or the housing placement of trans prisoners.

Enforcement has started and is documented as inconsistent. On 6 December 2025 Department of Public Safety troopers identity-checked people at women's restrooms outside the state Capitol; trans women holding female ID markers were admitted. Protests followed at the Capitol, the Austin City Council moved to circumvent the law's intent, and opponents warn that unclear guidelines produce uneven and invasive enforcement.

On 27 April 2026 Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a second complaint escalating the state investigation of Austin ISD over its bathroom policy, with a renewed records demand after a tip-line complaint. It is the first state enforcement inquiry into a school district under the bathroom law.

A national legal risk assessment dated July 2026 places Texas in the top "Do Not Travel" tier for adult trans travellers, alongside Florida, Idaho and Kansas, four states in all. The grading is applied law by law across care bans, bathroom bans and enforcement posture, using a five-year legislation-tracking methodology.

State identity documents are closed to change. House Bill 229 (Women's Bill of Rights), passed in May 2025, signed in June 2025 and effective September 2025, defines female as a person who can biologically produce ova and male as one who can biologically fertilize ova, requires people with disorders of sex development to select one binary gender with no third-gender recognition, applies across all state statutes, regulations and laws using gendered terms, and explicitly bars any change of sex on Texas driver's licences and birth certificates. Before this, changing the gender indicator on a birth certificate required a court order, with judicial discretion often referencing WPATH Standards of Care and a narrative statement from a doctor or therapist that the change was appropriate and in the person's best interest; no specific treatment, including surgery, was required. On 30 January 2025 Governor Abbott separately directed state agencies to recognise only two genders.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned. Senate Bill 14, signed in June 2023, follows a February 2022 Attorney General opinion classifying such care as child abuse and Governor Abbott directives ordering the Department of Family and Protective Services to investigate parents who facilitate it and imposing criminal penalties for a knowing failure to report. Five district attorneys refused to follow the directives. A March 2022 temporary injunction, reinstated by the Third Court of Appeals after an ACLU and Lambda Legal suit on behalf of providers including Dr. Megan Mooney and a family with a 16-year-old transgender girl on puberty blockers, blocked the policy. Investigative supervisor testimony in that litigation stated that trans-child cases faced different rules, with mandatory investigation regardless of evidence and a prohibition on discussing them by email or text.

Custody exposure is documented in Gibson v. Collier. Vanessa Lynn Gibson, a transgender woman incarcerated by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice and diagnosed with gender dysphoria, was denied gender-confirmation surgery because the agency's treatment policy excluded the procedure. The federal district court denied the state's immunity defences but ruled against her on the Eighth Amendment claim; the Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding there was no deliberate indifference and that refusing the surgery was a permissible medical choice under Kosilek, with Judge Barksdale dissenting on summary-judgement procedure.

Protection machinery is thin. The Texas hate-crime statute enhances penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, and it is rarely prosecuted. As of 2021 no state law barred discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations or insurance; Texas courts recognised the federal Bostock employment protections in March 2021. Cities including Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano and San Antonio prohibit gender-identity discrimination in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations, with narrower city-employment or public-accommodation protections in Denton, El Paso, Arlington, Brownsville, Corpus Christi, Houston, Irving, Lubbock, Mesquite and Waco.

Schools are a further site of exposure. The Parents' Bill of Rights of June 2025 bars school employees from teaching or discussing gender identity, bans LGBT-related student organisations, mandates deadnaming and misgendering of trans students, and expands parental authority. Since 1 September 2025 a law explicitly listing banned DEI school and certain workplace programmes for sexual orientation is in effect and is under court challenge.

Further measures are pending or unresolved. A prefiled House Bill 643 of November 2022 would expand the definition of sexually oriented businesses to restrict any performance where a performer uses clothing, makeup or other markers to exhibit gender variance from birth-assigned sex while performing, which would capture transgender performers in any role and criminalise minors' attendance at drag shows. Around fifty bills filed in early January 2023 sought to criminalise youth gender-affirming care, reduce adult access, bar sex-marker changes for minors and further restrict sports participation for trans and gender-nonconforming people.
tangentialFactors:
Texas sits in the same top "Do Not Travel" tier as Florida, Idaho and Kansas in the July 2026 assessment, a four-state group graded by the same law-by-law methodology. The tier reflects cumulative care bans, bathroom bans and enforcement posture rather than any single statute, so the Texas rating is a comparison of regime type, not a measure of incident frequency.

The legislative pipeline feeding the regime is documented across several sessions: around fifty bills filed in early January 2023 targeting youth care, adult access, sex-marker changes and sports participation; 2021 House Bill 1399 and Senate Bill 1311, passed 18-13, which would have revoked the licences of doctors providing blockers to minors; and the prefiled November 2022 House Bill 643 on gender-variant performance. House Bill 1106 excludes a parent's refusal to affirm a child's gender identity or sexual orientation from the child-abuse definition, which cuts against the February 2022 opinion's framework.

Adjacent measures affecting the same population include an October 2020 internal policy permitting social-worker discrimination against LGBT clients, the February 2022 removal of The Trevor Project from state suicide-prevention resources, the June 2019 religious-freedom law SB 1978 barring adverse government action for supporting religious organisations that may refuse LGBTQ service, a November 2025 constitutional parental-rights amendment, and a rule effective in 2025 under which judges refusing same-sex weddings on religious grounds face no punishment. The DEI statute in force since 1 September 2025 is under court challenge, so its scope may shift.

Comparison with the national picture: federal hate-crime law covers gender identity while the Texas statute does not, and 22 states plus the District of Columbia outlaw gender-identity discrimination where Texas does not. Texas therefore supplies fewer state-level protections than the federal floor in employment under Bostock, while adding state-level restrictions that federal law does not impose.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statewide statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing, public accommodations or insurance as of 2021, and bills on the subject have died in committee repeatedly since at least 1999. Protection depends on municipal ordinances of varying breadth, with the widest in Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano and San Antonio and narrower city-employment or public-accommodation rules elsewhere; Houston's broad 2014 ordinance was repealed by voters in 2015.

For Texas residents, the change route for birth certificates and driver's licences is closed by HB 229, effective September 2025, which explicitly bars any change of sex on those documents. The prior route required a court order supported by a narrative statement from a doctor or therapist, with judicial discretion often referencing WPATH Standards of Care and no specific treatment mandated.

The hate-crime statute enhances penalties for sexual-orientation-motivated crimes only and is rarely prosecuted, leaving gender-identity-motivated crime to ordinary charging. Federal Bostock employment protections apply and were recognised by Texas courts in March 2021, even as Texas joined a 2022 federal suit to overturn some LGBT protections.

Family recognition for residents: any adult may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, and legally married same-sex couples can adopt jointly and obtain supplemental birth certificates listing both parents. Lesbian couples may access IVF and assisted insemination, though health-plan IVF coverage requiring fertilisation with the spouse's sperm restricts access, and even federally funded adoption agencies may discriminate on religious beliefs. There is no statewide recognition of domestic partnerships for same- or opposite-sex couples; Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, El Paso, Houston and San Antonio provide health insurance to domestic partners of city workers, Travis, El Paso and Bexar Counties allow partner participation, and Pflugerville ISD allows inclusion at full worker cost. A 2001 Houston proposition barred city domestic-partner benefits except for legal spouses, and an April 2013 Attorney General opinion held that the constitution bars political-subdivision benefits based on domestic-partnership status.

Residents raising trans children face mandatory DFPS investigation under the February 2022 opinion framework and criminal penalties for a knowing failure to report, notwithstanding the March 2022 injunction and its reinstatement by the Third Court of Appeals. In schools, the Parents' Bill of Rights of June 2025 requires deadnaming and misgendering of trans students and bans LGBT-related student organisations.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Texas-specific count or rate of violence against trans people, and no denominator against which such a figure could be read, so no prevalence claim is made here.

The status of the prefiled House Bill 643 on gender-variant performance is unresolved: the source describes a November 2022 prefiled bill and does not report whether it advanced, was enacted or lapsed.

The outcome of the court challenge to the DEI statute in force since 1 September 2025 is not sourced; the record states only that it is under challenge.

Gibson v. Collier is reported through a secondary reference accessed 4 October 2026, and the underlying filing and appellate dates are not given in the inventory.

The nondiscrimination baseline is stated as of 2021 in the source; whether any statewide gender-identity discrimination statute was enacted between that snapshot and the present is not sourced here.

Whether DPS or state agencies have issued written guidance resolving the enforcement uncertainty reported after 6 December 2025 is not documented; the record notes only that opponents warn guidelines remain unclear.
